/WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 241 PM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026

Overview: A wet period will continue through Wednesday night with 
conditions very slowly turning drier from northwest to southeast 
across the state from Thursday into Friday morning. Looking at the 
weather elements to monitor from yesterday's discussion, it does 
seem that the first surge of atmospheric moisture plays more with 
the southern Canadian prairie shortwave and thus limits its 
northward potential. In part as a result of this is why the last few 
runs of the AIFS/AIGFS have trended a bit southward in the area of 
highest rainfall. 

Details: For Wednesday, there will be a steady stream of rainfall 
with rumbles of thunder ongoing over a good portion of Iowa outside 
of some southern areas as waves of strong low level thermodynamic 
forcing and steady kinematic forcing prevail over the state. 
Further, the remnant moisture from Hurricane Polo will arrive and 
keep precipitable water values above the 90th percentile and likely 
above sounding climatology record values with warm cloud depths 
unseasonably high for late September/early October. To compare, 
these heavy rainfall parameters are more reminiscent of summer time 
values. While the 850-300mb flow will be on the faster side (around 
30-40 knots), there looks to be a corridor where rainfall will 
repeat. As mentioned, there have been some shifts southward in the 
AI guidance as well as the deterministic and ensemble. However, 
there remain outliers in the heavy rainfall axis with the REFS/AIGFS 
(despite shifting southward recently) farther north over northwest 
and north central Iowa while the ECMWF/EPS is farther south over 
southern Iowa with the remainder of guidance in-between. So 
while the rounds of rainfall will waver and wiggle in their 
placement at times, there will be a band of 2 to 4 inches and 
locally 5 inches or more in some sort of southwest to northeast 
orientation. Looking at this rainfall probabilistically through 
Thursday morning, our forecast chances of 2" or more are above 
80% around an axis from near Mason City to Fort Dodge to Omaha 
with 4" or more around an axis from Omaha that ends near Fort 
Dodge. This rainfall may lead to flash flooding or at a minimum 
low lying and poor drainage flooding. In addition, areal or 
overland flooding may result as the soils continue to lose soil 
infiltration capacity.

Of course, this rainfall will route to area streams and rivers. As 
briefly mentioned in the short term discussion, soil conditions are 
wet with NASA SPoRT showing above the 70th percentile in the top 4" 
(rapid response layer) and 16" (river response layer) over most 
areas south of Highway 3 in central Iowa. Most rivers are above 
their baseflows (+2 feet above) from the start of the month, mainly 
areas along Highway 30 and southward in the state, but also much of 
the Cedar Basin. This is shown nicely by the National Water Model's 
14 day streamflow anomaly analysis. Thus, rivers and streams in 
north central into northwest Iowa have more capacity to handle the 
incoming rainfall and its runoff and routing compared to elsewhere. 
This includes the Winnebago, much of the upper Iowa and upper Des 
Moines (above Fort Dodge/FODI4) basins, and parts of the Skunk Basin 
(above Ames/AESI4). While these latter basins have more capacity, 
the 72 hour contingency hydrologic forecasts show rises across 
central Iowa with about a dozen forecast points rising above flood 
stage. This is also shown in last evening's experimental Hydrologic 
Ensemble Forecasting Service (HEFS), which uses ensemble GFS QPF, 
with several points exceeding flood stage at the 50% chance 
exceedance level. If looking at the 30% chance exceedance level (so 
higher QPF), this increases to over a dozen points above at least 
flood stage.

Moving later Thursday into Friday, the longwave trough deamplifies 
and largely shears out as an approaching northern stream wave aids 
in pushing this system away from the area. For sensible weather, 
this will mean the rain ending from early Thursday or perhaps as 
soon as Wednesday night over northwestern Iowa and our northwest 
forecast area. This drying trend moves slowly southeastward ending 
the rain in our southeastern forecast area by Friday morning.The 
approaching northern stream wave will move through Saturday and will 
bring a return of some clouds and atmospheric moisture return, but 
showers seem more limited and would certainly be progressive. Behind 
this system, northwesterly flow looks to take over and with a zone 
of high pressure moving in, this may spell a change as we continue 
into October with some drier conditions.
